messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is an 18-year-old police officer who came to see me after a colleague noticed he was flinching at roll call and suggested he talk to someone. He agreed only because he was afraid his reactions might get him or someone else hurt. He is tall and broad-shouldered, with a careful stillness that feels like it costs him something to maintain. He speaks quietly, measuring each word, and he told me he has not told anyone the full story of what he witnessed as a child.

When Kofi was seven years old, living with his mother and her boyfriend in a small apartment in Atlanta, he watched the boyfriend beat his mother over the course of an evening that felt like it lasted for days. He remembers it as a series of snapshots, each one frozen and vivid: the boyfriend’s hand coming down, his mother’s body hitting the kitchen linoleum, the sound of a chair scraping, the sudden silence that fell between her screams. He remembers the silence most of all. It came after the boyfriend left, and it was thick and wrong, and Kofi stayed in his corner behind the couch, his body curled tight, not moving, not breathing, waiting for something worse to happen. He stayed there for hours. His mother did not call the police. She told him never to speak of it, and he never did.

Now, eleven years later, Kofi works a job that requires him to walk into unfamiliar buildings and approach strangers. He told me he cannot do it without scanning every room for potential weapons. He notices knives on countertops, the shape of a screwdriver in someone’s hand, the way a person’s jacket might hide something. He does not do this consciously. It is simply that his eyes go there first, before he registers anything else about a person’s face. When a call comes in and dispatch sends him to a house he has never been to, his chest tightens and he has to force himself to get out of the squad car. He has come to believe that he cannot rely on himself in those moments, that his body will freeze or his mind will go blank, and that he will fail to stop something bad from happening. He is certain that bad things happen because he is not capable of preventing them.

At home, he lives alone in a studio apartment. He keeps the lights on at all times. Silence unsettles him. When the building goes quiet, he feels a pressure building, as though something dangerous is about to break through. He plays music or the television constantly, even while he sleeps. He has stopped seeing friends because they want to meet at bars or restaurants he does not know, and the thought of walking into a place where he cannot see all the exits or assess the people makes him feel as though he is about to lose his mind. He told me that his reactions since the event must mean he is going crazy, because normal people do not feel this way about a living room.

When memories of that night come to him, and they come often, he feels his body lock into the same position he held as a child: knees pulled to his chest, arms wrapped around his shins, head down. He told me that even if he is standing in the middle of the precinct, his body will try to fold itself, and he has to grip a desk or a doorframe to stay upright. Along with the posture comes a wave of grief so heavy he cannot breathe. He does not cry. He learned not to. But he feels the grief in his chest like a physical weight, and he is terrified that one day it will not pass.

What finally brought him to seek help was an incident last week. He was patrolling alone at night and stopped a car that had been driving erratically. The driver was a woman, and her passenger was a man who was yelling at her. Kofi asked the man to step out of the vehicle. The man refused. Kofi felt his body begin to curl, right there on the street, and he had to step back and tell dispatch he needed backup. He stood in the dark, heart pounding, certain he was about to fall apart in front of everyone. He did not. Backup arrived, and the situation was handled. But Kofi is now afraid that next time, his body will not cooperate. He wants to stop feeling like he is seven years old again, trapped behind a couch, waiting for the silence to end.
